title: OSI & TCP/IP Models
summary: Every network message crosses the same stack of jobs. Learn the 7 OSI layers, the 4-layer TCP/IP map, and how encapsulation glues them together.

blocks.markdown:
Networks are complex, so engineers broke the problem into **layers** — each layer doing one job and handing off to the next.

- The **OSI model** has 7 layers and is used as a teaching reference.
- The **TCP/IP model** has 4 layers and is what the real internet runs on.
- Understanding layers helps you pinpoint where a problem lives and which protocol fixes it.

Layering lets each part of a system change independently.

- A layer only talks to the layer **above** and **below** it — not across the stack.
- You can swap Wi-Fi for Ethernet at the bottom without touching HTTP at the top.
- It also means different vendors' hardware can talk: both obey the same layer contracts.

This isolation is why a web browser works over Wi-Fi, cable, or 5G without knowing the difference.

The OSI model stacks 7 layers, each with a distinct job.

<<< Image: OSI 7-layer stack (numbered 7 at top to 1 at bottom) beside the TCP/IP 4-layer stack, arrows showing the mapping (Application+Presentation+Session → Application; Transport → Transport; Network → Internet; Data Link+Physical → Network Access). Data flowing down the left side labelled 'sender adds headers', flowing up the right labelled 'receiver strips headers'. Clean dark-blue palette, generous whitespace. >>>

- Layer 7 **Application** — user-facing protocols (HTTP, SMTP, DNS).
- Layer 6 **Presentation** — data format, encryption, compression.
- Layer 5 **Session** — opens, manages, and closes connections between apps.
- Layer 4 **Transport** — end-to-end delivery, reliability (TCP/UDP).
- Layer 3 **Network** — routing across networks using IP addresses.
- Layer 2 **Data Link** — node-to-node framing on a single link (MAC addresses).
- Layer 1 **Physical** — raw bits on cables, radio waves, or fiber.

blocks.subTitle: Mnemonic
blocks.markdown:
A classic mnemonic for remembering the layers top-down (7 → 1):

**A**ll **P**eople **S**eem **T**o **N**eed **D**ata **P**rocessing

- **A**pplication, **P**resentation, **S**ession, **T**ransport, **N**etwork, **D**ata Link, **P**hysical.

Bottom-up version: **P**lease **D**o **N**ot **T**hrow **S**ausage **P**izza **A**way.

The **TCP/IP model** (also called the Internet model) was designed around the real protocols that power the internet. It merges some OSI layers.

- **Application** — merges OSI layers 5, 6, 7 (HTTP, DNS, SMTP, TLS).
- **Transport** — same as OSI layer 4 (TCP, UDP).
- **Internet** — same as OSI layer 3 (IP, ICMP).
- **Network Access** (Link) — merges OSI layers 1 and 2 (Ethernet, Wi-Fi).

Some texts list 5 layers by splitting Network Access into Physical + Data Link.

blocks.subTitle: OSI vs TCP/IP at a glance
blocks.markdown:
How the two models map to each other.

| TCP/IP layer | OSI layers | Key protocols |
|---|---|---|
| Application | 7 + 6 + 5 | HTTP, DNS, TLS, SMTP |
| Transport | 4 | TCP, UDP |
| Internet | 3 | IP, ICMP, ARP |
| Network Access | 2 + 1 | Ethernet, Wi-Fi |

OSI is the **reference**; TCP/IP is the **implementation**.

**Encapsulation** is how data travels down the sender's stack: each layer wraps the payload from the layer above in its own **header** (sometimes a trailer).

- Application writes data → Transport adds a **segment** header (port numbers).
- Network adds a **packet** header (IP addresses).
- Data Link adds a **frame** header + trailer (MAC addresses).
- Physical converts the whole thing to **bits**.

The chunk at each layer has its own name — called a **PDU** (Protocol Data Unit): segment, packet, frame, bit.

blocks.subTitle: De-encapsulation (receiver side)
blocks.markdown:
On the receiver's side the process reverses — **de-encapsulation**.

- Physical receives bits and passes raw frames up.
- Data Link strips the frame header, passes the packet up.
- Network strips the IP header, passes the segment up.
- Transport strips the TCP header, delivers data to the application.

Each layer only reads and removes **its own** header — it never touches headers that belong to other layers.

Real protocols map cleanly to layers — knowing this helps you troubleshoot.

- **Layer 7** — HTTP/HTTPS ([http-https](http-https)), FTP, SMTP, DNS.
- **Layer 4** — TCP (reliable, ordered), UDP (fast, no guarantee).
- **Layer 3** — IP (routing), ICMP (ping/traceroute), ARP (IP→MAC).
- **Layer 2** — Ethernet, Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11).
- **Layer 1** — cables (Cat6), fiber, radio signals.

See [network-fundamentals](network-fundamentals) for IP addressing basics.

Network hardware operates at a specific layer — that tells you what it can read.

- **Hub** — Layer 1. Repeats all bits to all ports, no intelligence.
- **Switch** — Layer 2. Reads MAC addresses, forwards frames to the right port.
- **Router** — Layer 3. Reads IP addresses, decides the next hop across networks.
- **Firewall / Load balancer** — Layer 4 or 7, inspects ports or full HTTP requests.

A switch can't read IP addresses; a router can't distinguish Wi-Fi from Ethernet at layer 1.

Common misconceptions:

- **"OSI is what the internet uses."** No — OSI is a reference model. The internet runs TCP/IP.
- **"TCP/IP has 7 layers."** No — it has 4 (or 5 in some textbooks). OSI has 7.
- **"Encapsulation adds data."** Only headers/trailers — the payload is unchanged.
- **"A router works at layer 2."** No — it reads IP (layer 3). Switches work at layer 2.

blocks.subTitle: Name the 7 OSI layers
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Name the 7 OSI layers and the job of each.**

7 Application — user protocols (HTTP, DNS). 6 Presentation — format/encrypt. 5 Session — open/close sessions. 4 Transport — end-to-end delivery (TCP/UDP). 3 Network — routing (IP). 2 Data Link — node-to-node framing (MAC). 1 Physical — raw bits.

Mnemonic top-down: **A**ll **P**eople **S**eem **T**o **N**eed **D**ata **P**rocessing.

blocks.subTitle: OSI vs TCP/IP
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between OSI and TCP/IP models?**

OSI is a **7-layer reference model** — a teaching tool, not a protocol. TCP/IP is the **4-layer model** the internet actually uses. OSI maps to TCP/IP: layers 5-7 → Application; layer 4 → Transport; layer 3 → Internet; layers 1-2 → Network Access.

blocks.subTitle: What is encapsulation?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is encapsulation in networking?**

As data travels **down** the sender's stack, each layer wraps it in a header (and sometimes a trailer) — segment → packet → frame → bits. The receiver **strips** each header going up. This is encapsulation/de-encapsulation, and it keeps layers independent.

blocks.subTitle: Router vs Switch layer
blocks.markdown:
**Q: At which OSI layer does a router operate? What about a switch?**

**Router — Layer 3** (Network). It reads IP addresses to route packets between networks. **Switch — Layer 2** (Data Link). It reads MAC addresses to forward frames within a network. A hub is Layer 1 — it just repeats bits blindly.
